title: Sponsor vs project manager through the life cycle
blurb: Explain how the sponsor's and project manager's responsibilities differ in every phase, from concept to benefits realisation.
question: A heritage trust is building a new visitor centre. The trust's director of operations is sponsor and an experienced project manager has been appointed. How do their responsibilities differ in each phase of the life cycle, and who is still accountable once the doors open and the PM has moved on?

teach.body: The SPONSOR is the individual accountable for the project's justification and its benefits: they own the business case, secure the funding, appoint the project manager, chair the board and take escalated decisions. The PROJECT MANAGER is responsible for delivering the agreed outputs within the agreed tolerances: planning, leading the team, controlling and reporting. Plain English: the sponsor asks 'are we doing the right project?' and the PM asks 'are we doing the project right?'

teach.h: Who is involved, and for how long
teach.caption: The sponsor's accountability runs through the extended life cycle; the PM's role ends at closure.

teach.body: The sponsor delegates tolerances (limits on time, cost, scope and so on) to the project manager. Inside those limits the PM manages risks and day-to-day problems without asking. When a problem is forecast to go beyond tolerance it becomes an ISSUE, and the PM escalates it to the sponsor with options and a recommendation. The sponsor decides, or takes it to the board. The PM provides the delivery evidence; the sponsor makes the business call.

steps.label: Forecast breach
steps.sub: Now an issue: beyond PM authority

steps.label: Sponsor decides
steps.sub: Or refers it to the board

teach.body: Concept: the sponsor builds the case (more visitors, more income) and appoints the PM, who helps test feasibility. Definition: the PM produces the plan and baseline; the sponsor approves them at the gate. Deployment: the PM runs the build; when piling costs threaten the cost tolerance he escalates and the sponsor releases contingency. Transition: the PM hands over and closes; the sponsor accepts and checks staff are trained. A year on, the sponsor reports visitor numbers to the trustees.

The split stays the same at heart. The sponsor still owns the business case and benefits, and agrees the fixed time and cost. But many day-to-day scope decisions move to the product owner, who prioritises the backlog and accepts each iteration. The project manager protects the time boxes, removes blockers and reports. The sponsor engages more often, typically at each release review, rather than mainly at phase gates.

teach.text: Classic traps: the PM PRODUCES the project management plan but the sponsor APPROVES it. The PM is responsible for outputs; the sponsor is accountable for benefits, which are mostly realised after the PM has left. And the PM never 'resolves issues within tolerance': an issue is by definition beyond tolerance and goes to the sponsor.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: State the core split: sponsor accountable for business case and benefits; PM responsible for delivery.
Walk through the phases the question names, one sponsor and one PM duty each.
Explain escalation: tolerances delegated down, issues escalated up.
Point out that benefits come after closure, so the sponsor stays accountable.
Use the scenario's details rather than generic statements.
Concept: sponsor initiates, owns business case, appoints PM; PM supports feasibility.
Definition: PM produces PMP and baseline; sponsor approves.
Deployment: PM delivers within tolerances; sponsor oversees and decides escalations.
Transition: PM hands over and closes; sponsor accepts and readies BAU.
Benefits realisation: sponsor accountable after the PM has gone.

summary: You can now explain how the sponsor's and project manager's responsibilities differ in each life cycle phase, and how escalation connects them. You can also explain why the sponsor stays accountable for benefits long after the project manager has closed the project.

A.q: During the Concept phase of a new leisure centre project, who initiates the project and owns its business case?
options: The project manager
The sponsor
The product owner
The senior supplier
A.why: In Concept the sponsor initiates the project, owns the business case and appoints the project manager.

whyNot.0: The PM supports feasibility work in Concept but does not own the business case.
whyNot.2: A product owner manages a backlog in iterative delivery, not the business case.
whyNot.3: The senior supplier represents suppliers on the board.

A.q: In the Definition phase, how are responsibilities for the project management plan (PMP) normally split?
options: Sponsor produces it; PM approves it
PMO produces it; users approve it
Board produces it; PM approves it
PM produces it; sponsor approves it
A.why: The PM produces the PMP and baseline in Definition; the sponsor approves them, usually at the gate into Deployment.

whyNot.0: This reverses the roles: the PM produces, the sponsor approves.
whyNot.1: The PMO may support planning, but the PM owns the PMP and the sponsor approves it.
whyNot.2: The board directs; it does not write the PMP, and the PM does not approve their own plan.

A.q: Eight months after a new customer relationship system was handed over, who is accountable for checking that the promised sales benefits are being realised?
options: The sponsor, with business managers
The PM, who stays on to track them
The supplier's delivery team leader
The PMO, which owns all the benefits
A.why: Benefits are mostly realised after handover, so the sponsor, working with business change managers and users, remains accountable for them.

whyNot.1: The PM's role normally ends at closure; benefits accountability sits with the sponsor.
whyNot.2: The supplier delivers outputs; it is not accountable for the buyer's benefits.
whyNot.3: A PMO may help track benefits, but accountability sits with the sponsor.

B.q: During Deployment, a supplier's insolvency means the project will exceed its cost tolerance. What should the project manager do?
options: Absorb the cost and tell no one
Ask the team to work unpaid overtime
Escalate to the sponsor with options
Cancel the contract and close the project
B.why: A forecast breach of tolerance is an issue, beyond the PM's authority. The PM escalates it to the sponsor with impact, options and a recommendation.

whyNot.0: Hiding a tolerance breach removes the sponsor's chance to decide and breaks governance.
whyNot.1: This is neither ethical nor within the PM's authority, and hides the issue.
whyNot.3: Closing the project is a sponsor or board decision, not the PM's.

B.q: During Transition, which statement correctly describes how the work is split?
options: Sponsor hands over; PM accepts the outputs
PM hands over; sponsor accepts, readies BAU
Users close the project; PM owns the benefits
Board hands over; supplier accepts outputs
B.why: In Transition the PM hands over the outputs and closes the project; the sponsor accepts them and makes sure business as usual is ready.

whyNot.2: The PM closes the project, and benefits belong to the sponsor.
whyNot.3: The board does not hand over, and the supplier is not the receiving organisation.

B.q: Complete the statement: 'The sponsor is ____ for the business case and benefits, while the project manager is responsible for delivering the agreed outputs.'
options: consulted
informed
independent
accountable
B.why: The sponsor is accountable: the single person who answers for the business case and the benefits.

whyNot.0: Being consulted means giving input, not owning the outcome.
whyNot.1: Being informed means being kept up to date, not owning the outcome.
whyNot.2: Independence is a quality of assurance, not the sponsor's relationship to the business case.

C.q: During Deployment of a payroll system, the sponsor attends every daily stand-up and reassigns developers' tasks. What is the BEST assessment?
options: The sponsor is doing the PM's job
The sponsor is owning the benefits
The sponsor is approving the baseline
The sponsor is giving good oversight
C.why: In Deployment the sponsor oversees, removes blockers and takes escalated decisions. Reassigning daily tasks is management, which undermines the PM.

whyNot.1: Benefits ownership is about the business case, not daily task allocation.
whyNot.2: Approving the baseline happens at the end of Definition, not at stand-ups.
whyNot.3: Oversight works through reports and escalations, not reassigning the team's tasks.

C.q: At the end of Definition the sponsor is on leave, so the PM signs supplier contracts and starts Deployment using the draft baseline. What is the main governance problem?
options: The PM did not consult the product owner
The users did not write the project plan
The PM made the sponsor's gate decision
The board should have produced the baseline
C.why: Approving the baseline and authorising Deployment is the sponsor's (or board's) decision at the gate. The PM has acted beyond their authority.

whyNot.0: A product owner is not the approver of a baseline or gate decision.
whyNot.1: Users give requirements; the PM produces the plan.
whyNot.3: The PM produces the baseline; the board or sponsor approves it.

C.q: On an iterative website project, which BEST describes the sponsor's role?
options: Prioritising the backlog each iteration
Owning the business case, time and cost
Running the team's daily stand-up meeting
Accepting each iteration's new features
C.why: In iterative work the sponsor still owns the business case and benefits and agrees the fixed time and cost; day-to-day priorities move to the product owner.

whyNot.0: Prioritising the backlog is the product owner's job.
whyNot.2: Daily stand-ups are run by the team and its PM or delivery lead.
whyNot.3: Accepting each iteration's work is the product owner's job.

reteach.title: Planning a wedding
reteach.question: A couple hire a wedding planner. Who is the sponsor, who is the project manager, and how do their jobs change from first idea to the years after the big day?

blocks.body: The couple are the sponsor: they decide whether to marry and what kind of day is worth paying for, set the budget and hire the planner. The planner is the project manager: draws up the plan, books suppliers, keeps to budget and runs the day. If the venue doubles its price, the planner rings the couple with options rather than deciding alone. After the day the planner moves on; the marriage (the benefit) is the couple's.

blocks.text: The planner never quietly spends beyond the agreed budget. Going outside the limit the couple set is their decision: in project terms, an issue escalated to the sponsor.

explain.body: The sponsor initiates the project, owns the business case and appoints the project manager. The PM supports feasibility work: options, early estimates and risks that feed the business case.

options: The PMO lead
The senior user
The sponsor
The team
test.why: The sponsor appoints the project manager, usually during Concept.

whyNot.0: A PMO may help find a PM, but the appointment is the sponsor's.
whyNot.1: The senior user represents users on the board; they don't appoint the PM.
whyNot.3: The team is led by the PM; they don't appoint them.

explain.body: The project manager produces the project management plan and the baseline (scope, schedule, budget). The sponsor reviews and approves them, normally at the gate that releases funding for Deployment.

test.q: What is the sponsor's main responsibility in the Definition phase?
options: Approving the plan and baseline
Writing the work breakdown structure
Producing the detailed task schedule
Testing the outputs before handover
test.why: In Definition the PM produces the plan and baseline and the sponsor approves them.

whyNot.1: The WBS is produced by the PM with the team.
whyNot.2: Detailed scheduling is the PM's work.
whyNot.3: Testing happens later and involves users and the team.

explain.body: The PM manages delivery within tolerances and reports progress. The sponsor oversees, removes blockers the PM cannot, and decides issues the PM escalates when a tolerance is forecast to be breached.

test.q: During Deployment, what is the sponsor's MAIN role?
options: Allocating tasks to each team member
Writing the weekly progress reports
Updating the risk register each day
Overseeing and deciding escalations
test.why: The sponsor oversees delivery, removes blockers and takes the decisions the PM escalates.

whyNot.0: Task allocation is the PM's management job.
whyNot.1: The PM writes progress reports for the sponsor.
whyNot.2: Maintaining the risk register is part of the PM's day-to-day control.

explain.body: The PM hands over the outputs and closes the project. The sponsor accepts them and ensures the business is ready to use them. Benefits are realised after closure, so the sponsor, with business change managers and users, stays accountable for them.

test.q: Why does the sponsor's accountability continue after the project closes?
options: The PM must report to them for a year
The sponsor must sign the final invoices
Benefits are realised after handover
The board is disbanded at project close
test.why: Most benefits come from using the outputs after handover, so someone in the business must stay accountable: the sponsor.

whyNot.0: The PM's role normally ends at closure.
whyNot.1: Financial close-down happens before closure; it is not why accountability continues.
whyNot.3: The board being disbanded doesn't explain the sponsor's continuing accountability for benefits.
